text: You're given a grid of zeros and ones. One is land, zero is water. There's exactly one island, and it has no lakes inside. Return the perimeter of the island.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the perimeter is the length of the outline around the land. Each land cell is a one-by-one square, and a side counts toward the perimeter only when the thing next to it is water or off the grid. Is that right?

Then here's the key idea. Each land cell has four sides. A side is on the perimeter if the neighbor on that side is water or out of bounds. A side shared with another land cell is inside, so it doesn't count. So the perimeter is just the total number of facing-out sides over all land cells. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The grid is up to a hundred by a hundred.

Let me run through the example. Take this small L-shape: three land cells, with water in the bottom-right corner. The three land cells face out on two, three, and three sides. That sums to eight, which is the perimeter.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to just scan every land cell and count its water or out-of-bounds sides directly. That already works in m times n time. This problem reminds me of a grid flood fill. Since it's a graph problem, I'll walk the island with DFS and count a perimeter edge every time I step off the island. Same complexity, and it's the reusable graph template.

Here's the plan. One: the DFS tries to step onto a cell. Two: if that cell is out of bounds or water, I add one edge and return. Three: if it's already marked minus one, I return; otherwise I mark it, so I never loop between neighbors, and try all four directions. One thing worth flagging — where the boundary check lives really matters. My first instinct was to skip a water or off-grid neighbor before recursing. That's a bug: stepping off the island is the event I'm counting, so with a pre-call guard the edge never gets added. The check has to be the base case inside the DFS. There's a trade-off here. The marker changes the input; if that's not allowed, I'd use a separate visited array, for m times n extra space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The outer loops find land and launch the DFS, which adds to res by reference. Inside the DFS, out of bounds or water adds one and returns, a visited cell just returns, and otherwise I mark the cell and walk all four directions with no guard. One thing worth flagging — the order in the base case matters. I check the bounds before I read the cell. Because the or short-circuits, an out-of-bounds cell returns early and I never touch the array out of range.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The same L-shape, starting at the top-left corner; expected output eight. The row that matters is the bottom-left cell: stepping right lands on the water cell and adds an edge, while stepping back up to the corner hits the visited check and adds nothing. Only the eight steps that land on water or off the grid add to res. Final answer eight. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. A single land cell returns four — all four steps go off the grid. A solid two-by-two block returns eight: the four inner sides are shared, so only the outer eight count.

The time complexity is m times n. Each land cell is marked once and its four sides are checked once. The space complexity is m times n for the recursion stack. In the worst-case scenario, a snake-shaped island that fills the grid makes the stack that deep. Oh, one more thing — this code already handles multiple islands for free. The outer loop starts a fresh DFS on any land cell not yet marked, and separate islands just add their perimeters into the same res. Nothing to change.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed the perimeter as the count of land sides facing out, right up front. You caught the real trap — that the boundary check has to be the base case inside the DFS, not a guard before the call, or the stepped-off edges never get counted. And you noted the bounds check must come before reading the cell because of short-circuit. Good work.
